objectives.text: Visit the starship control room and accept the Wilting Stream mission
Collect a plant sample from each of the three sites west of the landing site ({{samples}}/3)
Take the samples to the laboratory, east of the control room
Test the pH of each sample ({{ph_tests}}/3)
Examine each sample under the microscope ({{scope_tests}}/3)
Report the source of the contamination at the terminal
Make the contaminated water neutral at the mixing bench

title: Starship Explorer
subtitle: Explore the planet, find out what is harming its plants, and prove it in the lab
description: A science mission for a group of students. They collect plant samples along a stream, test them in the starship laboratory, and work out the source of a contamination.

actions.text: Use the arrow keys or click to walk. Head east to find the rocket.
Click the moon rover to ride it.

actions.content:
Have you ever looked up at the night sky and wondered if there are other planets out there beyond our solar system? Well, guess what? There are! They're called exoplanets!

Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars outside of our own solar system, just like Earth orbits around the Sun. Scientists use special telescopes to search for these faraway planets, and they've found thousands of them already!

Some exoplanets are similar to Earth, while others are very different. Some are super hot because they orbit close to their star, while others are freezing cold because they're far away. Some exoplanets even have weird names like "Hot Jupiter" or "Super-Earth"!

Finding exoplanets helps scientists learn more about the universe and whether there might be other places where life could exist. Who knows, maybe one day we'll even visit these distant worlds ourselves!
This console will take you to the planet below.

Mission: The Wilting Stream

Survey drones report that plants along a stream west of the landing site are dying, and nobody knows why.

Your job: collect a plant sample from three places along the stream, bring them to the ship's laboratory, and find the source of the problem using evidence.

Mission: Rescue Zam

Zam is stranded in a cave. Use your knowledge of levers and pulleys to save him!

Mission: The Wilting Stream

Samples collected: {{samples}}/3
Tests completed: {{tests_done}}/6
Science score: {{science_score}}/5

The sample sites are west of the landing site. The laboratory is through the door on the east side of this room.

Captain Vega: Welcome aboard! The mission consoles are along the back wall. The laboratory is through the east door, the observation deck is up the ramp, and the lift on the west side takes you back to the planet.

Mission accepted

Take the rocket lift back to the planet (walk off the west side of this room), then head west from the landing site and follow the stream.

Your checklist is at the top right of the screen. A good scientist compares, so look carefully at how each site is different.

actions.text: The plants here are drooping, and the stream looks cloudy.

actions.content:
Sample: marsh plant

You snip a few leaves and seal them in a jar with some water from the stream beside the plant.

What you observe: The leaves are limp and brown with yellow spots. The stream water here is cloudy and has a sharp, sour smell.

actions.text: These plants might be worth studying. The starship crew will know what to do.

actions.name: lander_note
actions.operand: cracked power cell dripping into the stream; water clear upstream, cloudy downstream

actions.content:
An old survey lander

It has been here a long time, half sunk beside the stream. A plate on its side reads POWER CELL: CORROSIVE ELECTROLYTE.

The orange power cell is cracked. Liquid drips from it into the stream.

What you observe: upstream of the lander (to the west) the water runs clear. Downstream (to the east) it turns cloudy.

Sample: gully plant

You snip a few leaves and seal them in a jar with some water from the stream beside the plant.

What you observe: This plant is just downstream of the old lander. It is the most badly wilted you have seen, and the water around its roots is cloudy.

actions.text: These plants might be worth studying. The starship crew will know what to do.

actions.content:
The spring

Water bubbles up out of the ground here. This is where the stream begins.

What you observe: the water is clear and has no smell. The plants around it stand tall.

Sample: meadow plant

You snip a few leaves and seal them in a jar with some water from the stream beside the plant.

What you observe: The leaves are firm and bright, and the stream water here is clear. This plant looks healthy.

actions.text: These plants might be worth studying. The starship crew will know what to do.

actions.content:
Think like a scientist

The mission is about plants that are dying. Why is it useful to collect a healthy plant as well?

call_to_actions.text: Healthy plants are easier to carry
It gives us something to compare the sick plants with
The lab only accepts healthy plants

actions.content:
Not quite

Easy to carry is not a scientific reason. A healthy sample is a control: something normal to compare against, so you can see what is different about the sick plants.

Correct!

Exactly. A healthy sample is a control. Whatever differs between it and the sick plants is a clue to the cause.

Not quite

The lab takes any sample. The healthy plant matters because it is a control: something normal to compare the sick plants against.

The laboratory

You set your three sample jars on the bench. Each jar holds leaves and some stream water from where the plant grew.

  • pH tester: measures how acidic or basic the water is.
  • Microscope: shows the plant cells up close.
  • Notebook: keeps your results in one table.
  • Mixing bench: try changing the pH of the stream water.
  • Report terminal: when all six tests are done, say what you think happened.

actions.content:
Report filed

Source: acid leaking from the old lander's power cell.

Science score: {{science_score}} out of 5.

Have you tried the mixing bench?

pH tester

Dip a fresh test strip into the water in a jar. The strip changes colour, and the colour tells you the pH.

Which jar?
All three samples have been through the pH tester. Your results are in the notebook.

Marsh sample

The strip turns yellow-orange: pH 4. The marsh water is acidic.

Gully sample

The strip turns orange: pH 3. The water just below the lander is strongly acidic, the most acidic of the three.

Meadow sample

The strip turns green: pH 7. The spring water is neutral, like pure water.

Before you test

The pH scale runs from 0 to 14. Pure water is 7.

If a test strip reads 3, what does that tell you about the water?

call_to_actions.text: It is neutral, like pure water

actions.content:
Correct!

Right. Numbers below 7 are acids, and the lower the number, the stronger the acid. Lemon juice is about 2.

Not quite

Neutral is exactly 7. A reading of 3 is well below that, which makes it a fairly strong acid.

Not quite

Bases are the numbers above 7. A reading of 3 is below 7, which makes it an acid.

Microscope

Put a thin slice of leaf on a slide and look at its cells. Also look for anything that should not be there, such as fungus threads or bacteria.

Which sample?
All three samples have been through the microscope. Your results are in the notebook.

actions.name: scope_marsh
actions.operand: shrunken cells, broken walls, no microbes

actions.content:
Marsh sample

The cells are shrunken and many cell walls are broken. You search carefully and find no fungus and no bacteria.

actions.name: scope_gully
actions.operand: badly shrunken cells, broken walls, no microbes

actions.content:
Gully sample

These cells are the worst damaged of all: shrivelled, with broken walls. Again there is no fungus and no bacteria.

Meadow sample

The cells are plump and green, packed neatly together, with intact walls. Nothing unusual.

What does the evidence say?

The sick plants have damaged cells, but you found no fungus and no bacteria in any sample.

What is the best conclusion?

call_to_actions.text: The plants caught an infection that spreads from plant to plant
Something in their surroundings is damaging them

actions.content:
Not quite

An infection is caused by living things such as fungus or bacteria, and you would expect to see them. You found none, so the evidence points away from infection and toward something in the plants' surroundings.

Correct!

Yes. With no microbes present, an infection is unlikely. The damage is more likely caused by something in the environment, such as the water the plants are growing in.

Not quite

The microscope showed the healthy sample perfectly well, so it works. The evidence is real: no microbes, which points toward something in the plants' surroundings.

Make a prediction

The beaker holds stream water from the gully. It is acidic.

What should you add to bring it back toward neutral (pH 7)?

call_to_actions.text: An acid, such as lemon juice
A base, such as baking soda

actions.content:
Not quite

Adding an acid makes water more acidic, so the pH goes down. A base does the opposite and cancels acid out. Try both and watch the number.

Correct!

Right. A base cancels out an acid. Scientists call this neutralising. Now test your prediction.

Not quite

Salt dissolves but does not change the pH. A base, such as baking soda, cancels out an acid. Try it and watch the number.

Mixing bench

The beaker of gully water now reads pH {{beaker_ph}}.

Add one drop at a time and watch what happens to the number.

call_to_actions.text: Add a drop of baking soda solution (a base)
Add a drop of lemon juice (an acid)

actions.content:
Neutral!

The beaker reads pH 7. Each drop of base cancelled out some of the acid. If the leak were stopped, the stream could recover in the same way.

Your report

Look at your notebook. Where do the sick plants grow, and what is different about the water there?

What is the most likely source of the contamination?

call_to_actions.text: A plant disease spreading along the stream
Acid leaking from the old lander's power cell into the stream
Too little sunlight in the gully and the marsh

actions.content:
Check the evidence

A disease would be caused by microbes, and the microscope showed none in any sample. Look again at the pH column in your notebook: what changes between the meadow and the gully?

Mystery solved

The evidence fits together:

  • Upstream of the lander the water is neutral and the plants are healthy.
  • Just below the lander the water is strongly acidic and the plants are worst.
  • Further downstream the acid is weaker, and the plants are sick but less so.
  • No microbes were found, so it is not an infection.

The cracked power cell is leaking acid into the stream. A repair crew is on its way.

Science score: {{science_score}} out of 5.

Check the evidence

All three sites are out in the open under the same sky, so sunlight is the same for each. A good explanation has to account for what is different between the healthy site and the sick ones. What did the pH tests show?
